primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic bacterial infection acquired when mucous membranes or abraded skin contact water or soil contaminated with urine from infected animals. Clinical disease can present with fever, headache, prominent myalgias, conjunctival suffusion, and gastrointestinal symptoms; severe disease can involve jaundice, acute kidney injury, respiratory failure, meningitis, or multiorgan dysfunction.
vignette: A 34-year-old man develops high fever, severe headache, and intense pain in both calves one week after helping clean flooded homes following a hurricane. He repeatedly waded through standing water that contained rodent debris and had several abrasions on his legs. Examination shows conjunctival suffusion without purulent discharge and scleral icterus. Laboratory studies show acute kidney injury and elevated bilirubin. He has no cough, dyspnea, rash, or focal skin ulcer.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Dengue can cause abrupt fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, rash, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia after mosquito exposure. The combination of contaminated floodwater exposure, severe calf myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, and kidney injury is more characteristic of leptospirosis.

Hepatitis A can cause fever, fatigue, abdominal symptoms, dark urine, and jaundice. It does not best explain the contaminated animal-urine water exposure together with severe calf myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, and acute kidney injury.

Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome follows exposure to infected rodent excreta and begins with fever and myalgia, making rodent exposure a plausible distractor. It classically progresses to cough, dyspnea, and pulmonary edema/capillary leak; this patient instead has the characteristic leptospirosis constellation of conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, renal injury, and floodwater exposure.

Ehrlichiosis is a tickborne febrile illness commonly associated with headache, malaise, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated aminotransferases. The exposure route and the combination of conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, renal injury, and marked calf myalgia are more supportive of leptospirosis.
key_expl: This patient most likely has leptospirosis. CDC states that Leptospira organisms are shed in the urine of infected animals and can persist in contaminated water or soil; risk rises after hurricanes, flooding, and heavy rainfall. Characteristic clinical clues include fever, headache, myalgia—often prominent in the calves—conjunctival suffusion, and, in severe disease, jaundice and kidney failure. The combination of floodwater exposure through abraded skin and this multisystem clinical pattern is highly characteristic.
objective: Recognize leptospirosis after exposure to water or soil contaminated by animal urine, particularly after flooding, when fever and severe myalgias occur with conjunctival suffusion and possible hepatic or renal dysfunction.
